drugs.name: Abemaciclib
groups: Oncology: Targeted Therapy (Kinase and Other Inhibitors)

f.adm.pO: Tablets swallowed whole with or without food, at about the same times each day
f.adm.specialAdministrationInstructions: Hazardous drug handling; tablets not crushed, chewed or split; grapefruit products are avoided per label
f.bd.whatItDoes: Blocks CDK4 and CDK6, stopping breast cancer cells from entering the DNA-copying phase.
f.bd.whatItIs: An oral targeted cancer pill for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, taken twice a day without a break week.
f.bd.whyItIsUsed: Used with endocrine therapy for high-risk early breast cancer and for advanced or metastatic HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, and alone after prior therapy.
f.ci.absoluteContraindications: No absolute contraindications listed in the label
f.ci.relativeContraindications: Active severe diarrhea, severe neutropenia, history of venous thromboembolism, interstitial lung disease, severe hepatic impairment, pregnancy
f.di.importantCombinationEffects: Tamoxifen combination adds VTE risk; additive myelosuppression
f.di.majorDrugInteractions: Strong CYP3A inhibitors (ketoconazole is avoided per label) raise exposure; strong and moderate CYP3A inducers lower exposure; abemaciclib inhibits renal transporters OCT2, MATE1 and MATE2-K, raising serum creatinine and possibly metformin levels
f.dose.adultDose: 150 mg orally twice daily in combination with fulvestrant, tamoxifen, imlunestrant or an aromatase inhibitor; 200 mg orally twice daily as monotherapy (label, HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer)
f.dose.hepaticDoseAdjustment: Severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C): dosing frequency reduced to once daily per label
f.dose.maximumDose: 200 mg twice daily as monotherapy; 150 mg twice daily in combination (label)
f.dose.renalDoseAdjustment: No adjustment for mild to moderate renal impairment; serum creatinine can rise without a true GFR change
f.dose.repeatDose: Continuous twice-daily dosing without a break week
f.home.whatDiseaseDoesThisSuggest: HR-positive breast cancer, early high-risk or metastatic.
f.home.whatEmergencyCouldThisMedicationCon: Dehydration and acute kidney injury, neutropenic infection, pulmonary embolism, pneumonitis.
f.home.whatHappensIfTheySuddenlyStopTaking: No withdrawal syndrome; tumor progression or recurrence is possible.
f.home.whatShouldEMSAskAbout: Number of loose stools, fluid intake, dizziness, leg swelling, chest pain, fever.
f.home.whyMightMyPatientBeTakingIt: Oral targeted therapy, usually with endocrine therapy.
f.ind.otherCommonIndications: Adjuvant treatment with endocrine therapy for HR-positive, HER2-negative, node-positive early breast cancer at high risk of recurrence (label)
f.ind.primaryIndications: HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer with an aromatase inhibitor as initial endocrine-based therapy, with fulvestrant after endocrine progression, or as monotherapy after endocrine therapy and prior chemotherapy in the metastatic setting; with imlunestrant for ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated advanced or metastatic breast cancer (FDA-authorized test) after progression on at least one line of endocrine therapy (label)
f.mem.memoryTrick: Abemaciclib is the CDK4/6 inhibitor of the gut: most diarrhea, least neutropenia, no week off, and it can be used alone.
f.mem.mostTestedFact: Among CDK4/6 inhibitors, abemaciclib causes the most diarrhea and the least neutropenia, is dosed continuously and can be used alone.
f.mem.oneSentenceSummary: Abemaciclib is a continuously dosed oral CDK4/6 inhibitor for HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, known for diarrhea.
f.mem.simpleExplanation: A twice-daily breast cancer pill that pauses cell division and often causes diarrhea.
f.moa.mechanismOfAction: Selective inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (more potent against CDK4) that prevents cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma protein (Rb), arresting cells in G1 before S phase; at higher concentrations inhibits other kinases, which allows single-agent activity and continuous dosing.
f.moa.physiologicEffects: G1 arrest of Rb-intact tumor cells; diarrhea from GI effects; milder neutropenia than other CDK4/6 inhibitors; creatinine rise from tubular transporter inhibition.
f.mon.labs: CBC, liver tests, creatinine, electrolytes during diarrhea
f.mon.otherMonitoring: Stool frequency, hydration, leg swelling or pain suggesting DVT
f.mon.spO2: Hypoxia with pulmonary embolism or pneumonitis
f.pearl.commonMedicationErrors: Interpreting the creatinine rise as true kidney injury without context; confusing the continuous schedule with the 3-weeks-on schedule of other CDK4/6 inhibitors.
f.pearl.dangerousCombinations: Strong CYP3A inhibitors such as ketoconazole.
f.pearl.highYieldClinicalPearl: Abemaciclib is the only CDK4/6 inhibitor approved as monotherapy and is dosed continuously; its adjuvant approval came from the monarchE trial.
f.pearl.whatEMSShouldKnow: Abemaciclib is the CDK4/6 inhibitor known for diarrhea, which usually starts within the first weeks; dehydration, acute kidney injury and electrolyte loss can follow, and it carries a VTE warning.
f.pearl.whatToCheckBeforeGiving: CBC, liver tests, VTE history, diarrhea status and pregnancy status are typically reviewed before starting.
f.pearl.whatToMonitorAfterGiving: Stool frequency, hydration, ANC, liver tests, dyspnea, leg swelling.
f.pearl.whenToStopAdministration: Grade 3 or 4 diarrhea, neutropenia, hepatotoxicity, VTE or pneumonitis are classic reasons for holding per label.
f.pk.metabolism: Hepatic CYP3A4 to active metabolites (M2, M18, M20)
f.se.commonSideEffects: Diarrhea, neutropenia, nausea, abdominal pain, fatigue, vomiting, anemia, decreased appetite, alopecia, increased creatinine
f.se.lifeThreateningAdverseEffects: Pulmonary embolism, severe pneumonitis, hypovolemic acute kidney injury from diarrhea
f.se.seriousSideEffects: Severe diarrhea with dehydration, febrile neutropenia, hepatotoxicity, venous thromboembolism, interstitial lung disease
f.sp.geriatrics: Similar efficacy; dehydration from diarrhea is a concern
f.sp.hepaticImpairment: Once-daily dosing in severe impairment per label
f.sp.lactation: Not recommended during therapy and for a period after the last dose per label
f.sp.pregnancy: Embryo-fetal toxicity; contraception during therapy and after the last dose per label
f.sp.renalImpairment: No adjustment in mild to moderate impairment
f.tox.overdosePresentation: Dehydration and electrolyte loss from diarrhea
f.tox.signsOfToxicity: Exaggerated adverse effects: diarrhea, neutropenia, fatigue
f.wp.importantPrecautions: Diarrhea is managed early with antidiarrheals and fluids per label; CBC and liver tests are reviewed before starting, every 2 weeks for the first 2 months, monthly for the next 2 months and as indicated per label.
f.wp.majorWarnings: Diarrhea, neutropenia, interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis, hepatotoxicity, venous thromboembolism, embryo-fetal toxicity, increased serum creatinine without a true change in kidney function (BUN, cystatin C or calculated GFR are used to judge kidney function instead).

drugs.edu: This targeted breast cancer pill is taken twice a day every day, usually with hormone therapy. Diarrhea is very common in the first weeks; at the first loose stool, the antidiarrheal medicine recommended by the care team and extra fluids are used, and diarrhea that does not settle is reported. Fever, leg swelling or pain, chest pain, shortness of breath or yellow skin are reported right away.
drugs.nurse: Diarrhea is typically managed at the first loose stool with an antidiarrheal and oral fluids per label, and grade 3 or 4 diarrhea or diarrhea needing hospitalization typically prompts holding and notifying the provider; CBC and liver tests are reviewed before starting, every 2 weeks for the first 2 months and monthly for the next 2 months per label; leg swelling, chest pain or dyspnea suggesting VTE or pneumonitis are reported to the provider; a creatinine rise can reflect transporter inhibition rather than true GFR loss

drugs.name: Adagrasib
groups: Oncology: Targeted Therapy (Kinase and Other Inhibitors)

f.adm.pO: Tablets swallowed whole, with or without food
f.adm.specialAdministrationInstructions: Hazardous drug handling; a missed dose is skipped if more than 4 hours late, and a vomited dose is not repeated per label
f.bd.whatItDoes: Binds the mutant KRAS G12C protein and keeps it switched off, stopping the tumor growth signal.
f.bd.whatItIs: An oral targeted cancer drug for tumors with the KRAS G12C mutation.
f.bd.whyItIsUsed: Used for previously treated KRAS G12C-mutated non-small cell lung cancer. The colorectal cancer use (with cetuximab) was removed from the FDA label in August 2026.
f.ci.absoluteContraindications: No absolute contraindications listed in the label
f.ci.relativeContraindications: Congenital long QT syndrome, baseline QTc prolongation, uncorrected electrolyte abnormalities, heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, active liver disease, pregnancy
f.di.alcoholInteraction: No specific interaction; adds to GI and hepatic effects
f.di.drugClassesToAvoid: Strong CYP3A4 inducers and inhibitors, sensitive CYP3A substrates with narrow therapeutic index, QT-prolonging drugs
f.di.importantCombinationEffects: Additive QT prolongation with ondansetron and other QT-prolonging drugs used for its nausea
f.di.majorDrugInteractions: Strong CYP3A4 inducers lower levels; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors raise levels; adagrasib strongly inhibits CYP3A4 (raises midazolam and other sensitive substrates) and inhibits CYP2C9, CYP2D6 and P-gp; QT-prolonging drugs
f.dose.adultDose: 600 mg orally twice daily until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity (label, single agent for KRAS G12C NSCLC)
f.dose.hepaticDoseAdjustment: No dose adjustment for mild to moderate hepatic impairment per label; labeled dose reductions for hepatotoxicity
f.dose.renalDoseAdjustment: No dose adjustment for mild to moderate renal impairment per label
f.home.whatDiseaseDoesThisSuggest: KRAS G12C-mutated non-small cell lung cancer, often advanced.
f.home.whatEmergencyCouldThisMedicationCon: Dehydration and electrolyte loss, torsades de pointes, hepatotoxicity, pneumonitis.
f.home.whatHappensIfTheySuddenlyStopTaking: No withdrawal syndrome; tumor progression is possible.
f.home.whatShouldEMSAskAbout: Vomiting, diarrhea, fainting or palpitations, new cough or shortness of breath, other medicines that affect heart rhythm.
f.home.whyMightMyPatientBeTakingIt: Long-term oral targeted therapy after earlier treatment.
f.id.pharmacologicClass: Kinase pathway inhibitor (covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor)
f.ind.offLabelUses: Other KRAS G12C-mutated solid tumors (off-label, investigational)
f.ind.otherCommonIndications: None in the current label (the colorectal cancer indication with cetuximab was removed from the label in 08/2026)
f.ind.primaryIndications: Adults with KRAS G12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC after at least one prior systemic therapy (label, accelerated approval)
f.mem.keyFact: 600 mg twice daily; strong CYP3A4 inhibitor itself.
f.mem.memoryTrick: Like sotorasib, adagrasib locks KRAS G12C in the off state.
f.mem.mostTestedFact: Covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor for previously treated NSCLC (accelerated approval); the colorectal cancer indication was removed from the label in 08/2026.
f.mem.oneSentenceSummary: Adagrasib is an oral covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor for previously treated NSCLC, limited by GI toxicity, QTc prolongation and hepatotoxicity.
f.mem.simpleExplanation: A twice-daily pill that switches off the broken KRAS G12C growth switch in some lung and colon cancers.
f.moa.mechanismOfAction: Covalent, irreversible inhibitor that binds the mutant cysteine 12 of KRAS G12C in the switch II pocket and locks KRAS in its inactive GDP-bound state, blocking RAF-MEK-ERK (MAPK) signaling and causing cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis; long half-life gives sustained target inhibition and it penetrates the CNS; it is also a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor of its own metabolism.
f.moa.physiologicEffects: Reduced MAPK signaling and tumor shrinkage including intracranial responses; GI toxicity, QTc prolongation, hepatotoxicity and pneumonitis are the main toxicities.
f.moa.receptorTarget: KRAS G12C (mutant GTPase, switch II pocket)
f.mon.eCG: Baseline and periodic QTc in patients at risk
f.pearl.commonMedicationErrors: Missing strong CYP3A4 interactions; adding QT-prolonging antiemetics without ECG review; confusing adagrasib with sotorasib dosing.
f.pearl.dangerousCombinations: QT-prolonging drugs, sensitive CYP3A substrates, strong CYP3A inducers.
f.pearl.highYieldClinicalPearl: Adagrasib has CNS penetration and a long half-life (about 23 hours) compared with sotorasib. Its earlier colorectal cancer approval (paired with cetuximab) was removed from the label in 08/2026.
f.pearl.whatEMSShouldKnow: Adagrasib is taken twice daily, prolongs the QTc and commonly causes vomiting and diarrhea, so electrolyte losses add to arrhythmia risk.
f.pearl.whatToCheckBeforeGiving: KRAS G12C test result, ECG, electrolytes, liver tests, interacting CYP3A and QT drugs and pregnancy status are typically reviewed before starting.
f.pearl.whatToMonitorAfterGiving: Vomiting, diarrhea and hydration, QTc and electrolytes, liver tests, respiratory symptoms.
f.pearl.whenToStopAdministration: QTc over 500 ms, grade 3 or 4 GI toxicity or liver test elevation and confirmed ILD are classic reasons for holding per label.
f.se.commonSideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, fatigue, musculoskeletal pain, hepatotoxicity, renal impairment (creatinine rise), edema, dyspnea, decreased appetite
f.se.lifeThreateningAdverseEffects: Torsades de pointes, fatal ILD, severe hepatotoxicity
f.se.seriousSideEffects: QTc prolongation, severe GI toxicity with dehydration, hepatotoxicity, pneumonitis/ILD
f.sp.geriatrics: No overall differences in safety reported
f.sp.hepaticImpairment: No adjustment in mild to moderate impairment; hepatotoxicity monitoring
f.sp.lactation: Not recommended during therapy and for 1 week after the last dose per label
f.sp.pregnancy: Embryo-fetal risk based on mechanism; use in pregnancy is generally deferred
f.sp.renalImpairment: No adjustment in mild to moderate impairment; creatinine rise is common
f.tox.overdoseTreatment: Supportive care, ECG and electrolyte monitoring
f.tox.signsOfToxicity: Exaggerated GI toxicity and QTc prolongation
f.wp.importantPrecautions: ECG and electrolytes are reviewed in patients at QT risk and when combined with QT-prolonging drugs; liver tests are reviewed before and monthly for 3 months then as clinically indicated per label; antiemetic and antidiarrheal support is typical.
f.wp.majorWarnings: Gastrointestinal adverse reactions (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, some severe), QTc interval prolongation, hepatotoxicity, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis.

drugs.edu: This targeted cancer medicine is taken by mouth twice a day, with or without food. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea are very common, and medicines to control them are often prescribed. Fainting, a racing or irregular heartbeat, yellow skin, or a new cough or shortness of breath are reported to the care team right away. Many other medicines interact with it, so a full medicine list is shared with each provider and pharmacist.
drugs.nurse: Adagrasib is a hazardous oral drug given as 600 mg twice daily per label; ECG, potassium and magnesium are reviewed in patients at QT risk, and QTc over 500 ms typically prompts holding and notifying the provider; vomiting and diarrhea are assessed for dehydration and electrolyte loss; liver tests are reviewed monthly for the first 3 months per label; adagrasib is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, so interacting drugs and QT-prolonging antiemetics are flagged

drugs.name: Carbidopa-Levodopa-Entacapone

f.adm.administrationRate: Not split; one whole tablet per dose
f.adm.specialAdministrationInstructions: Patients already on separate carbidopa/levodopa plus entacapone 200 mg switch to the matching strength per label
f.bd.whatItDoes: Levodopa becomes dopamine in the brain; carbidopa and entacapone stop it being broken down in the body so more reaches the brain and lasts longer.
f.bd.whatItIs: A single tablet combining levodopa, carbidopa and entacapone for Parkinson disease.
f.bd.whyItIsUsed: Used for Parkinson disease, often when doses of carbidopa/levodopa wear off before the next dose.
f.ci.relativeContraindications: Severe psychosis, history of melanoma, angle-closure glaucoma, severe cardiovascular or pulmonary disease, peptic ulcer history
f.di.importantCombinationEffects: Entacapone plus catecholamine infusions can increase heart rate and arrhythmia risk
f.di.majorDrugInteractions: Nonselective MAO inhibitors (hypertensive risk), dopamine antagonists such as antipsychotics and metoclopramide (reduced effect), drugs metabolized by COMT such as isoproterenol, epinephrine, dopamine, dobutamine (exaggerated heart rate and arrhythmia), iron salts (chelation)
f.dose.adultDose: One tablet at each dosing interval, each strength containing 200 mg entacapone; maximum 8 tablets per 24 hours (6 tablets for the 50/200/200 strength); daily dose individualized by titration (label, Parkinson disease)
f.dose.hepaticDoseAdjustment: Hepatic impairment reduces entacapone clearance; caution per label
f.dose.maximumDose: 8 tablets per 24 hours for most strengths; 6 tablets for the 50/200/200 strength (label)
f.dose.renalDoseAdjustment: No specific renal adjustment in label
f.dose.repeatDose: Dosing interval matches the patient's carbidopa/levodopa schedule
f.home.whatDiseaseDoesThisSuggest: Parkinson disease, often several years into treatment with wearing off
f.home.whatEmergencyCouldThisMedicationCon: Falls, orthostatic syncope, psychosis, parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome after missed doses
f.home.whatHappensIfTheySuddenlyStopTaking: Severe rigidity and a neuroleptic malignant syndrome-like state with fever and confusion
f.home.whatShouldEMSAskAbout: Time of last dose, missed doses, falls, hallucinations
f.id.pharmacologicClass: Dopamine precursor plus aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase inhibitor plus COMT inhibitor
f.ind.eMSPrehospitalIndications: Recognition of a Parkinson medication in falls, hallucinations, or a missed-dose rigidity crisis
f.ind.otherCommonIndications: Replacement of separately given carbidopa/levodopa and entacapone, or for end-of-dose wearing off (label)
f.mem.memoryTrick: Stalevo = stay level: carbidopa and entacapone both stop levodopa breakdown outside the brain; entacapone turns urine orange and causes diarrhea.
f.mem.mostTestedFact: Carbidopa blocks peripheral DOPA decarboxylase and entacapone blocks peripheral COMT, increasing levodopa entering the brain; entacapone causes orange urine and diarrhea.
f.mem.oneSentenceSummary: Carbidopa-levodopa-entacapone combines a dopamine precursor with DOPA decarboxylase and COMT inhibitors for Parkinson disease wearing off.
f.mem.simpleExplanation: One pill with three parts that refills brain dopamine and helps each dose last longer.
f.moa.mechanismOfAction: Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier via the large neutral amino acid transporter and is decarboxylated to dopamine in the striatum; carbidopa inhibits peripheral aromatic L-amino acid (DOPA) decarboxylase without crossing the blood-brain barrier; entacapone reversibly inhibits peripheral catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), reducing conversion of levodopa to 3-O-methyldopa and prolonging levodopa half-life.
f.moa.physiologicEffects: Improved bradykinesia and rigidity, longer on time and less end-of-dose wearing off, more dyskinesia, less peripheral nausea than levodopa alone.
f.moa.receptorTarget: Dopamine D1 and D2 receptors (via dopamine), DOPA decarboxylase (peripheral), COMT (peripheral)
f.mon.labs: Vitamin B6 level before starting therapy (label); periodic liver tests and CBC in long-term use
f.pearl.commonMedicationErrors: Splitting tablets or confusing strengths, which differ by carbidopa/levodopa content but share 200 mg entacapone.
f.pearl.dangerousCombinations: Haloperidol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine (dopamine antagonists), nonselective MAOIs.
f.pearl.highYieldClinicalPearl: Entacapone is a peripheral COMT inhibitor that turns urine brownish orange and extends each levodopa dose.
f.pearl.whatEMSShouldKnow: Missed doses can produce rapid rigidity and immobility, and abrupt withdrawal can cause hyperthermia and confusion resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
f.pearl.whatToCheckBeforeGiving: Dose timing, recent changes and any missed doses are relevant history.
f.pearl.whatToMonitorAfterGiving: Rigidity, temperature, orthostatic blood pressure, mental status.
f.pearl.whenToStopAdministration: Hyperthermia with rigidity after missed doses or hallucinations with agitation are classic red flags.
f.pk.duration: Several hours, longer than levodopa alone
f.pk.elimination: Levodopa metabolites renal; entacapone mainly biliary (feces)
f.pk.halfLife: Levodopa about 1.5 hours with carbidopa and entacapone; entacapone about 0.4 to 0.7 hours (beta phase)
f.pk.metabolism: Levodopa decarboxylation and O-methylation; entacapone glucuronidation
f.se.commonSideEffects: Dyskinesia, nausea, diarrhea, urine discoloration, dizziness, abdominal pain, hallucinations, somnolence
f.se.lifeThreateningAdverseEffects: Hyperpyrexia and confusion resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome after abrupt withdrawal; rhabdomyolysis
f.se.seriousSideEffects: Orthostatic hypotension, psychosis, impulse control disorders, sleep attacks, falls
f.sp.geriatrics: Higher risk of hallucinations, orthostasis and falls
f.sp.lactation: Levodopa can suppress lactation; entacapone excretion unknown
f.sp.pregnancy: Animal data show harm; limited human data
f.tox.overdoseTreatment: Supportive care, ECG monitoring, airway and cardiovascular support
f.tox.signsOfToxicity: Agitation, dyskinesia, hallucinations, hypertension or hypotension, tachycardia; urine and sweat discoloration
f.wp.importantPrecautions: Entacapone turns urine brownish orange; high-protein meals and iron supplements reduce levodopa absorption.
f.wp.majorWarnings: Falling asleep during activities of daily living, hyperpyrexia and confusion on rapid dose reduction or withdrawal, dyskinesia, hallucinations and psychosis, impulse control disorders, orthostatic hypotension, diarrhea and colitis, possible melanoma risk, rhabdomyolysis, vitamin B6 deficiency (seizures reported that were refractory to usual anti-seizure medicines and resolved only after vitamin B6).

drugs.edu: This tablet combines three Parkinson medicines and is taken one tablet at each dose time, swallowed whole. Urine may turn brownish orange, which is harmless. Large protein meals and iron pills can reduce how well it works. Stopping suddenly can cause stiffness and fever, and sudden sleepiness, hallucinations or strong urges like gambling are worth reporting.
drugs.nurse: Each strength contains 200 mg entacapone, so only one tablet is given per dosing interval and the maximum is 8 tablets per 24 hours (6 for the 50/200/200 strength) per label; dose timing is typically kept precise to avoid wearing off; abrupt reduction can cause a neuroleptic malignant syndrome-like state; dopamine antagonists such as haloperidol and metoclopramide oppose its effect; orthostatic blood pressure and fall risk are commonly reviewed
cites: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed): Carbidopa, Levodopa and Entacapone
FDA Drug Safety Communication (Mar 20, 2026): FDA Is Requiring Warning about Vitamin B6 Deficiency and Associated Seizures for Drug Products Containing Carbidopa/Levodopa

drugs.name: Carbidopa/Levodopa

f.adm.specialAdministrationInstructions: Dose times matter: delays cause freezing and rigidity.
f.bd.whatItDoes: Levodopa is converted to dopamine in the brain; carbidopa prevents conversion outside the brain.
f.di.majorDrugInteractions: Antipsychotics and metoclopramide (block dopamine), MAOIs, iron (absorption)
f.ind.eMSPrehospitalIndications: Recognize: abrupt stopping causes parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome
f.mem.memoryTrick: Levodopa becomes dopamine in the brain; carbidopa stops it converting outside, cutting nausea. Doses are time-critical; haloperidol or metoclopramide block it.
f.mem.oneSentenceSummary: Carbidopa/levodopa replaces dopamine; never stop abruptly and avoid dopamine blockers.
f.mem.simpleExplanation: The main Parkinson's medicine that refills brain dopamine.
f.moa.mechanismOfAction: Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and becomes dopamine; carbidopa blocks peripheral DOPA decarboxylase (less nausea, more brain delivery).
f.mon.otherMonitoring: Temperature; vitamin B6 level before starting therapy (label)
f.pearl.highYieldClinicalPearl: Missed doses in hospitals cause harm: give on time.
f.pearl.whatEMSShouldKnow: Avoid dopamine blockers (haloperidol, droperidol, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine) in Parkinson's patients. Do not miss doses.
f.wp.importantPrecautions: Protein meals reduce absorption. Vitamin B6 levels are evaluated before starting; low B6 is supplemented, and treatment can start or continue while supplementing (label).
f.wp.majorWarnings: Abrupt stopping or rapid dose reduction can cause an NMS-like syndrome; hallucinations; impulse-control disorders; dyskinesias; vitamin B6 deficiency, with seizures reported that did not respond to usual anti-seizure medicines and resolved only after vitamin B6.

drugs.edu: Take this medicine at the same times each day; a high-protein meal can reduce how well it works. Stand up slowly to prevent dizziness. Your urine or sweat may turn dark, which is harmless. Report uncontrolled movements, hallucinations, sudden sleep episodes, or new urges to gamble or shop.
drugs.nurse: Assess BP lying and standing and monitor for orthostatic hypotension; Assess motor symptoms, wearing-off, and dyskinesias; time doses consistently; Do not give with nonselective MAO inhibitors (stop at least 14 days before); Avoid dopamine antagonists such as haloperidol and metoclopramide; Do not stop abruptly due to risk of hyperpyrexia and confusion resembling NMS
cites: FDA prescribing information (DailyMed): Carbidopa and Levodopa
2019 AGS Beers Criteria (American Geriatrics Society, updated 2023)
FDA Drug Safety Communication (Mar 20, 2026): FDA Is Requiring Warning about Vitamin B6 Deficiency and Associated Seizures for Drug Products Containing Carbidopa/Levodopa

drugs.name: Ferric Carboxymaltose

f.adm.administrationRate: IV push about 100 mg/min; infusion at least 15 minutes
f.adm.dilutionPreparation: Diluted in 0.9% sodium chloride to at least 2 mg iron/mL for infusion
f.adm.iV: Slow IV push at about 100 mg per minute, or infusion over at least 15 minutes per label
f.adm.specialAdministrationInstructions: Observation for hypersensitivity at least 30 minutes; avoiding extravasation
f.bd.whatItDoes: Delivers iron that macrophages release to transferrin to rebuild iron stores and hemoglobin.
f.bd.whatItIs: An IV iron given in two large doses about a week apart.
f.bd.whyItIsUsed: Used for iron deficiency anemia when oral iron is not tolerated or does not work, in CKD not on dialysis, and for iron deficiency in heart failure.
f.ci.absoluteContraindications: Hypersensitivity to Injectafer or its components (label)
f.ci.relativeContraindications: Pre-existing hypophosphatemia, risk factors such as vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, hyperparathyroidism or repeated dosing; iron overload
f.di.drugClassesToAvoid: Other parenteral iron at the same time
f.di.importantCombinationEffects: Repeated courses are associated with cumulative hypophosphatemia
f.di.majorDrugInteractions: Oral iron (reduced absorption during IV therapy)
f.dose.adultDose: 750 mg IV in two doses separated by at least 7 days (total 1,500 mg per course) for patients 50 kg or more, or alternatively 15 mg/kg up to 1,000 mg as a single dose; 15 mg/kg per dose in two doses under 50 kg (label, iron deficiency anemia)
f.dose.infusionDose: Undiluted slow IV push or diluted infusion
f.dose.maximumDose: 750 mg per dose in the two-dose regimen; 1,500 mg per course (label)
f.dose.pediatricDose: 15 mg/kg IV in two doses separated by at least 7 days for patients under 50 kg (label)
f.dose.repeatDose: Second dose at least 7 days later; repeat course if anemia recurs
f.home.whatDiseaseDoesThisSuggest: Iron deficiency anemia or heart failure with iron deficiency.
f.home.whatHappensIfTheySuddenlyStopTaking: No withdrawal; iron deficiency can recur.
f.home.whatShouldEMSAskAbout: Recent IV iron, allergic symptoms, bone pain or weakness.
f.ind.offLabelUses: Iron deficiency in pregnancy (second and third trimester), inflammatory bowel disease, perioperative anemia (guideline-based)
f.ind.primaryIndications: Iron deficiency anemia in adults and pediatric patients 1 year and older with intolerance or unsatisfactory response to oral iron; iron deficiency anemia in adults with non-dialysis CKD; iron deficiency in adults with heart failure (NYHA II/III) to improve exercise capacity (label)
f.mem.keyFact: Label warning for symptomatic hypophosphatemia (FGF23 mediated).
f.mem.memoryTrick: CARBOXYmaltose robs phosphate: this IV iron raises FGF23, which makes the kidneys waste phosphate and can cause symptomatic hypophosphatemia.
f.mem.mostTestedFact: IV irons with high single doses; ferric carboxymaltose causes hypophosphatemia through FGF23.
f.mem.oneSentenceSummary: Ferric carboxymaltose is an IV iron given as 750 mg twice at least 7 days apart, with a label warning for symptomatic hypophosphatemia.
f.mem.similarDrugs: Ferric derisomaltose, iron sucrose, ferumoxytol, iron dextran
f.mem.simpleExplanation: A large-dose IV iron given in two shots a week apart.
f.moa.mechanismOfAction: Polynuclear iron(III) hydroxide core stabilized by a carboxymaltose shell; the tightly bound complex is taken up by reticuloendothelial macrophages, which release iron to transferrin for erythropoiesis or store it as ferritin; it also raises intact FGF23, increasing renal phosphate wasting.
f.moa.physiologicEffects: Rise in hemoglobin, ferritin and transferrin saturation; improved functional capacity in heart failure with iron deficiency; urinary phosphate loss with hypophosphatemia.
f.moa.receptorTarget: Reticuloendothelial system; transferrin and ferritin; FGF23 effect
f.mon.bloodPressure: Transient hypertension during or after dosing
f.mon.labs: Hemoglobin, ferritin, transferrin saturation; serum phosphate in at-risk patients
f.mon.otherMonitoring: Bone pain, muscle weakness, fatigue from hypophosphatemia; injection site
f.pearl.commonMedicationErrors: Giving the second dose too soon; repeated courses without phosphate review; extravasation.
f.pearl.dangerousCombinations: Other parenteral iron at the same time.
f.pearl.highYieldClinicalPearl: Ferric carboxymaltose raises intact FGF23, so hypophosphatemia is far more frequent than with ferric derisomaltose or iron sucrose.
f.pearl.whatEMSShouldKnow: Ferric carboxymaltose replaces large iron deficits in two doses and has a label warning for symptomatic hypophosphatemia, which can be severe and prolonged.
f.pearl.whatToCheckBeforeGiving: Allergy history, phosphate level, prior IV iron, heart failure status.
f.pearl.whatToMonitorAfterGiving: Blood pressure, hypersensitivity signs, phosphate, bone pain.
f.pearl.whenToStopAdministration: Hypersensitivity leads to discontinuation per label; symptomatic hypophosphatemia leads to evaluation and treatment.
f.se.commonSideEffects: Nausea, hypertension, flushing, injection site reactions, hypophosphatemia, headache
f.se.lifeThreateningAdverseEffects: Anaphylaxis; severe prolonged hypophosphatemia with osteomalacia and fractures
f.se.seriousSideEffects: Symptomatic hypophosphatemia, hypersensitivity, extravasation skin staining
f.sp.lactation: Small amounts in milk; generally considered compatible
f.sp.pediatrics: Labeled for iron deficiency anemia from 1 year of age
f.sp.pregnancy: Used in the second and third trimesters when oral iron fails; severe reactions can cause fetal bradycardia
f.sp.renalImpairment: No adjustment; labeled in non-dialysis CKD
f.tox.overdoseTreatment: Supportive care; chelation for iron overload
f.tox.toxicDoseToxicity: Iron overload with doses beyond need
f.wp.boxedWarning: Boxed warning: symptomatic hypophosphatemia. Injectafer can cause severe, prolonged low phosphate with serious outcomes (hospitalization, osteomalacia, fractures), including in patients with normal baseline phosphate and no risk factors. Serum phosphate is checked before a repeat course in at-risk patients and in anyone getting a repeat course within 3 months, and low phosphate is corrected before dosing (label).
f.wp.importantPrecautions: Patients are observed for hypersensitivity for at least 30 minutes after dosing; extravasation can cause long-lasting brown skin staining.
f.wp.majorWarnings: Symptomatic hypophosphatemia with osteomalacia and fractures (serum phosphate is reviewed before a repeat course in at-risk patients per label), hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis, transient hypertension with flushing, laboratory interference with serum iron for 24 hours.

drugs.edu: This iron is given by IV, usually as two doses at least a week apart. Staff watch for allergic reactions for at least 30 minutes afterward, and blood pressure can rise briefly with flushing. Bone pain, muscle weakness or ongoing tiredness weeks later can be from low phosphate and are worth reporting. A brown skin stain can occur if the IV leaks.
drugs.nurse: Hypersensitivity signs and blood pressure are observed for at least 30 minutes after dosing per label; serum phosphate is reviewed before a repeat course in patients at risk of hypophosphatemia per label; the second dose is given at least 7 days after the first; extravasation causes long-lasting brown skin discoloration, so the IV site is watched closely
cites: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
FDA Drug Safety Communication (Sept 1, 2026): FDA Adds Boxed Warning to Labeling for Ferric Carboxymaltose Injection (Injectafer) to Describe Risk of Low Phosphate Levels

drugs.name: Tirzepatide

f.bd.whatItDoes: Activates GIP and GLP-1 receptors, boosting insulin, lowering glucagon, slowing digestion, and reducing appetite.
f.bd.whatItIs: A weekly dual-hormone injection for diabetes and weight loss.
f.bd.whyItIsUsed: Type 2 diabetes (including lowering the risk of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death in high-risk patients), obesity, and obstructive sleep apnea with obesity.
f.dose.pediatricDose: 10 yr and older (type 2 DM): 2.5 mg SQ weekly x 4 wk, then 5 mg weekly; increase by 2.5 mg after at least 4 wk as needed; max 10 mg weekly
f.id.pharmacologicClass: Dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist
f.ind.eMSPrehospitalIndications: Recognize: GI side effects, pancreatitis, aspiration risk
f.ind.primaryIndications: Type 2 diabetes (adults and children 10 yr and older); reduce risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (CV death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke) in adults with type 2 diabetes at high risk (Mounjaro label, 08/2026); chronic weight management; OSA with obesity
f.mem.memoryTrick: Tirzepatide is the TWO-hormone shot, GIP plus GLP-1, for diabetes and weight loss; like GLP-1 drugs it is boxed for thyroid C-cell tumors.
f.mem.oneSentenceSummary: Tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist for T2DM and obesity.
f.mem.simpleExplanation: A weekly dual-hormone shot for sugar and weight.
f.moa.physiologicEffects: Lower glucose, large weight loss, nausea.
f.pearl.highYieldClinicalPearl: Dual agonist: greatest weight loss among current agents.
f.sp.pediatrics: Established for type 2 DM in age 10 yr and older (max 10 mg weekly)
f.wp.importantPrecautions: Delayed gastric emptying: aspiration risk. Reduces oral contraceptive absorption.
f.wp.majorWarnings: Pancreatitis, gallbladder disease, AKI, diabetic retinopathy complications (temporary worsening with rapid glucose improvement in patients with a history of retinopathy).

drugs.edu: Inject under the skin once a week on the same day, with or without food. Nausea, diarrhea and decreased appetite are common at first. Report severe belly pain, signs of dehydration, or a lump or swelling in your neck, and use a backup birth control if you take the pill.
drugs.nurse: Assess personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2 (contraindicated); monitor glucose, especially with insulin or sulfonylureas; hold and notify for signs of pancreatitis or gallbladder disease; monitor hydration and renal function with GI losses; counsel on reduced oral contraceptive effectiveness after initiation and dose increases.
cites: American Diabetes Association. Standards of Care in Diabetes (2025)

items.text: New use: lowering the risk of heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk. New warning: diabetic eye disease can briefly worsen when blood sugar improves quickly.
items.name: Tirzepatide

items.text: New warning: low vitamin B6 can cause seizures that may not respond to the usual seizure medicines. A vitamin B6 level is checked before starting.
items.name: Carbidopa/Levodopa

items.text: The same new vitamin B6 and seizure warning as carbidopa-levodopa.
items.name: Carbidopa-Levodopa-Entacapone

items.text: New boxed warning: severe, long-lasting low phosphate, which can lead to bone softening and fractures.
items.name: Ferric Carboxymaltose

items.text: New use with imlunestrant for certain advanced breast cancers. Also noted: it raises serum creatinine without truly lowering kidney function.
items.name: Abemaciclib

items.text: The colorectal cancer use was removed from the label. The lung cancer use is unchanged.
items.name: Adagrasib

q.q: A patient's medication list includes carbidopa/levodopa. Which ALS drugs should be avoided if possible?
q.a: Haloperidol or droperidol
w: Ondansetron
Fentanyl
Normal saline
q.x: Dopamine blockers worsen Parkinson's disease.

q.q: A patient with Parkinson's disease becomes rigid, febrile, and confused after missing several levodopa doses. This is most likely:
q.a: Parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome
w: Normal aging with mild dehydration and fatigue
Hypoglycemia from poor intake
Opioid overdose from pain pills
q.x: This syndrome follows abrupt levodopa withdrawal, so levodopa should never be stopped abruptly.

q.q: Which antiemetic is safest for a patient with Parkinson's disease?
q.a: Ondansetron
w: Metoclopramide
Prochlorperazine
Droperidol
q.x: Dopamine-blocking antiemetics worsen Parkinson's symptoms and should be avoided.

q.q: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson's disease is vomiting. His medications include carbidopa/levodopa and apomorphine injections. Which is the best decision about ondansetron?
q.a: Withhold ondansetron because of the apomorphine
w: Give ondansetron 4 mg IV as for any adult
Give ondansetron ODT, since the oral form is safe
Give ondansetron and a fluid bolus together
q.x: Ondansetron with apomorphine can cause profound hypotension and loss of consciousness, so it is contraindicated. Changing the route does not remove the interaction.

q.q: A resident with Parkinson's disease is very shaky and stiff late in the afternoon. The CNA should:
q.a: Report the change to the nurse
w: Give the resident's next dose early
Tie the resident's hands to stop shaking
Tell the resident to try harder to move
q.x: Symptoms can return when the medicine wears off. The nurse needs to know so timing can be reviewed.

q.q: A resident on carbidopa-levodopa gets dizzy when standing. The CNA should:
q.a: Have the resident stand up slowly
w: Have the resident jump up quickly
Keep the resident in bed all day
Walk the resident without a gait belt
q.x: This medicine can cause low blood pressure when standing. The resident should rise slowly, and fall precautions should be used.

q.q: Which instruction should the nurse reinforce for a client taking carbidopa-levodopa?
q.a: Avoid high-protein meals at the time of doses
w: Take it with a high-protein meal each time
Expect the urine to turn bright blue or green
Stop it suddenly if dizziness occurs
q.x: Protein competes with levodopa for absorption; urine or sweat may darken. The drug should never be stopped abruptly.

q.q: A resident with Parkinson disease takes her medicine on a strict schedule. Why does timing matter?
q.a: Late doses can leave her unable to move or swallow safely
w: It helps the kitchen plan her meal trays around the dose times
It reduces the monthly cost of her medicine at the pharmacy
It keeps the medicine from tasting bitter when she takes it
q.x: Parkinson medicines wear off, and a late dose can leave a resident frozen and at risk when eating or walking.

q.q: A 68-year-old man with Parkinson disease takes levodopa combined with carbidopa. What does carbidopa contribute?
q.a: Inhibits peripheral DOPA decarboxylase
w: Inhibits central DOPA decarboxylase
Inhibits peripheral COMT activity
Inhibits central monoamine oxidase B
q.x: Carbidopa does not cross the blood-brain barrier and blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, lowering nausea and increasing CNS delivery.

q.q: What is carbidopa/levodopa used to treat?
q.a: Parkinson's disease symptoms like tremor and stiffness
w: Memory loss from Alzheimer's disease
Seizures from epilepsy
Dizziness from inner ear problems
q.x: Carbidopa/levodopa replaces dopamine in the brain to ease Parkinson's symptoms such as shaking, stiffness, and slow movement. It does not treat memory loss or seizures.

q.q: A resident who takes carbidopa/levodopa has new jerky, twisting movements of the arms and face that they cannot control. What should the nursing assistant do?
q.a: Report the new movements to the nurse
w: Restrain the arms to keep them still
Ignore it because it is part of aging
Encourage the resident to sleep it off
q.x: Uncontrolled jerky or twisting movements (dyskinesias) are a known side effect of carbidopa/levodopa and need to be reported. Restraining the resident is unsafe.

q.q: Which teaching about carbidopa-levodopa is correct?
q.a: Large high-protein meals can reduce its effect
w: It must be taken with a high-protein shake
It works best when taken with iron pills
It cures Parkinson disease over time
q.x: Dietary protein competes with levodopa for absorption, so large protein meals can weaken its effect. Iron supplements also reduce absorption, and the drug treats symptoms but does not cure Parkinson disease.

q.q: Why is carbidopa combined with levodopa in Parkinson disease?
q.a: It blocks peripheral DOPA decarboxylase so more levodopa reaches the brain
w: It blocks central MAO-B so dopamine breakdown slows
It directly stimulates dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum
It inhibits COMT so levodopa is converted to dopamine faster
q.x: Carbidopa does not cross the blood-brain barrier; it inhibits peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine, increasing CNS delivery and reducing nausea. COMT inhibition is the mechanism of entacapone, a different add-on.

q.q: Why is carbidopa combined with levodopa in Parkinson disease?
q.a: It blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa to dopamine
w: It directly stimulates central dopamine receptors
It inhibits monoamine oxidase B in the brain
It blocks central muscarinic receptors
q.x: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase and does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so more levodopa reaches the brain and peripheral nausea is reduced. MAO-B inhibition describes selegiline and rasagiline.

q.q: Which teaching is appropriate for a patient taking carbidopa-levodopa?
q.a: Large high-protein meals may reduce how well it works
w: High-protein shakes boost its effect
Its full effect is felt minutes after the first dose
It works best when taken with iron supplements
q.x: Dietary protein competes with levodopa for absorption and transport into the brain, so large protein loads near doses can blunt its effect. Iron also reduces levodopa absorption.

q.q: A patient with Parkinson disease takes carbidopa/levodopa at 8 AM. When is gait training usually best scheduled?
q.a: During peak 'on' time, often about 1 hour after the dose
w: Right before the next dose is due
Immediately after a high-protein breakfast
Late evening when the drug has worn off
q.x: Motor performance is best when levodopa is at a good level; coordinating with dose times improves session quality.

q.q: Why is carbidopa combined with levodopa?
q.a: It blocks peripheral conversion of levodopa so more reaches the brain
w: It directly stimulates dopamine receptors
It slows dopamine breakdown in the brain
It blocks acetylcholine to reduce tremor
q.x: Carbidopa inhibits peripheral dopa decarboxylase, reducing nausea and increasing brain levodopa.

q.q: A patient eats a high-protein lunch right before a levodopa dose and is rigid during afternoon therapy. Best explanation?
q.a: Dietary amino acids compete with levodopa for absorption and transport
w: Protein converts levodopa to dopamine in the gut
Protein causes dopamine receptors to shut down
High protein causes peak-dose dyskinesia
q.x: Large neutral amino acids share transporters with levodopa; spacing protein away from doses can help, which should be discussed with the provider or dietitian.

q.q: Writhing, dance-like movements that appear when levodopa levels are highest are called:
q.a: Peak-dose dyskinesia
w: Wearing-off tremor
Freezing of gait
Akathisia from withdrawal
q.x: Peak-dose dyskinesia reflects excess dopamine stimulation and becomes more common with years of levodopa use.

q.q: A patient's tremor and slowness return an hour before each scheduled dose. This pattern is called:
q.a: Wearing off
w: Peak-dose dyskinesia
On-state freezing
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
q.x: End-of-dose wearing off is the most common motor fluctuation; the timing pattern should be documented and reported.

q.q: During an 'off' period, which therapy focus is most appropriate?
q.a: Safety, cueing strategies and stretching
w: High-level balance perturbation training
Maximal treadmill speed testing
Introducing a complex new motor skill
q.x: Off periods limit motor learning and raise fall risk; demanding training fits best in the 'on' state.

q.q: Which serious reaction can follow abrupt loss of levodopa therapy, for example when doses are missed during a hospital stay?
q.a: High fever, severe rigidity and confusion resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome
w: Sudden drop in muscle tone with flaccidity
Rapid improvement in gait
Isolated mild headache
q.x: Abrupt withdrawal can cause a parkinsonism-hyperpyrexia syndrome, a medical emergency; missed doses should be reported.

q.q: Entacapone is added to carbidopa/levodopa mainly to:
q.a: Extend the duration of each levodopa dose
w: Replace levodopa entirely
Treat orthostatic hypotension
Reduce dyskinesia by blocking dopamine
q.x: COMT inhibitors slow levodopa breakdown, reducing wearing off; they may increase dyskinesia and can tint urine orange-brown.

q.q: A patient on carbidopa/levodopa becomes lightheaded on standing at the start of therapy. What should the therapist measure?
q.a: Orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate
w: Grip strength
Peak expiratory flow
Two-point discrimination
q.x: Levodopa and Parkinson disease itself both cause orthostatic hypotension, a major fall risk.

q.q: In Parkinson's disease, when are speech and swallowing usually best?
q.a: During the 'on' period after a levodopa dose
w: During the 'off' period before a dose
Only on waking in the morning
Only late at night
q.x: Motor function, including speech and swallowing, often improves when levodopa is working; sessions are often timed to 'on' periods.

q.q: A patient with Parkinson's develops 'wearing off' before each dose. How might this appear in therapy?
q.a: Softer voice and slower swallow near the next dose
w: Improved loudness right before the next dose
Excess drooling only during 'on' time
Stuttering that appears only after meals
q.x: As levodopa wears off, hypophonia, reduced articulation and dysphagia can return; reporting the pattern helps the team.

q.q: A 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and BMI 39 kg/m2 takes metformin. A1c is 8.2 percent. She wants a medication that maximizes both glucose lowering and weight loss. She has no personal or family history of thyroid cancer. Which is most appropriate?
q.a: Tirzepatide
w: Glimepiride
Pioglitazone
Insulin detemir
q.x: Dual GIP and GLP-1 agonist therapy with tirzepatide provides very high glucose-lowering efficacy and the greatest weight loss among diabetes agents.

q.q: A patient on tirzepatide and glipizide has lost weight and now logs several low readings. What is the best explanation?
q.a: Improved glucose control plus the sulfonylurea is raising hypoglycemia risk
w: Tirzepatide alone commonly causes severe lows
The glucometer is broken
Weight loss always raises blood glucose
q.x: GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 agonists rarely cause lows alone, but combined with insulin or sulfonylureas they can. The pattern should be reported for medication review.
